question: A student claims: "Every continuous function is differentiable." Examine the validity of the statement using the function $f(x)=|x|$ at $x=0$.
explanation:
Checking continuity at $x=0$
$$\lim_{x\to 0^-}|x|=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to 0^+}|x|=0$$
Also, $f(0)=0$. Hence, $$\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)=f(0)$$ so $f$ is continuous at $x=0$.
Checking differentiability at $x=0$
The left-hand derivative is $$\lim_{h\to 0^-}\frac{|h|}{h}=-1$$ and the right-hand derivative is $$\lim_{h\to 0^+}\frac{|h|}{h}=1$$
These are unequal, so $f$ is not differentiable at $x=0$.
Conclusion
The statement is false. A function may be continuous at a point without being differentiable there.

options.A: The statement is true because $|x|$ is both continuous and differentiable at $x=0$.
options.B: The statement is true because continuity always implies equality of one-sided derivatives.
options.C: The statement is false because $|x|$ is neither continuous nor differentiable at $x=0$.
options.D: The statement is false because $|x|$ is continuous at $x=0$ but its left-hand and right-hand derivatives are $-1$ and $1$ respectively.
